Suffuse

suh-FYOOZ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To suffuse to gradually spread through or over something, especially with light, color, or a feeling.

The old kitchen was suffused with the smell of cinnamon every time she baked.

Worked Example

Pride suffused the coach's voice as he described his team's comeback season.

The pride didn't arrive all at once -- it spread gradually through everything he said, which is exactly what suffuse describes.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — touch → suffuse → flood

touch vs. suffuse

touch vs. suffuse: To touch someone with an emotion is a light, brief impact; to suffuse them with it means the feeling spreads through everything they do.

flood vs. suffuse

flood vs. suffuse: To be suffused with a feeling is a slow, spreading process; to be flooded with it happens all at once and completely overwhelms you.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — suf-

prefix — suf-: under, up from below (Latin (sub-))

root — fuse

root — fuse: to pour, melt together (Latin (fundere))

Put it together

Put it together: Suffuse comes from Latin sub- ('up from below') + fundere ('to pour') -- literally 'to pour up from underneath,' capturing how a quality seems to well up and spread through something.

Use the root in a new word: transfuse

Use the root in a new word: transfuse: The same fundere root gives us confuse (to 'pour together' ideas until they're muddled) and transfuse, to 'pour across' from one container to another.

Root Check

Word Choice

Suffuse almost always takes a passive or intransitive form ('suffused with,' 'suffuse through') rather than an active one -- you don't usually suffuse an object the way you'd paint it.
